1.title: CDMP FUNDAMENTALS
1.text: Welcome to Module 8: Data Integration and Interoperability — often abbreviated DII. This is Chapter 8 of the DMBOK, worth about six percent of the exam. This chapter is all about how data moves and gets consolidated across systems — the world of ETL, message queues, and service buses. There are several precise distinctions the exam tests, like ETL versus ELT and the different latency types, so let's get them straight. Here we go.

1.title: Module Overview & Learning Objectives
1.text: Here's our plan. You'll define Data Integration and Interoperability and learn to distinguish integration from interoperability — they're related but not identical. You'll list the six latency types and the three interaction models. You'll compare ETL with ELT and learn the transformation types. You'll understand Change Data Capture, the Enterprise Service Bus, Service-Oriented Architecture, Complex Event Processing, and the canonical model. You'll be able to apply the point-to-point interface formula. And you'll recognize the five activities, plus governance and metrics. Let's start with the definition.

1.title: Definition & Goals
1.text: The DMBOK defines Data Integration and Interoperability as the processes related to the movement and consolidation of data within and between data stores, applications, and organizations. Now, two related terms that the exam likes to separate. Interoperability is the ability of multiple systems to communicate with each other. Integration is about consolidating data in one place, resolving inconsistencies, and converting data to common formats. There are three goals: make data available in the format and timeframe that consumers need; lower the cost and complexity of solutions by developing shared models and interfaces; and ensure critical data is available where and when needed, securely and reliably. The one-line distinction: integration consolidates, interoperability communicates.

1.title: Business Drivers
1.text: What drives the need for DII? Several things. Accessing data scattered across multiple systems and sources. Reducing the cost of moving and converting data. Adhering to regulatory requirements. Aligning data with business needs and providing accurate, timely information for decisions. Supporting migration away from legacy systems. And enabling Master Data Management. The big-picture point is that DII is the foundational plumbing beneath many other initiatives — you can't do Master Data Management, build a data warehouse, or migrate off a legacy system without solid data integration underneath it all.

1.title: The 3 Guiding Principles
1.text: DII rests on three guiding principles. First, design for re-use — build your approaches and solutions for maximum reuse, so that transformation code and mappings remain stable even as source and target systems change around them. Second, abstraction — separate the interface from the implementation, which lets multiple sources and targets interact through a single interface rather than custom-wiring each one. And third, shared responsibility — DII requires cooperation between technical and business teams, where the business data stewards validate the transformation rules and the technical teams implement them. Re-use, abstraction, shared responsibility — three principles that all push toward maintainable, collaborative integration.

1.title: Latency — The 6 Types
1.text: Latency is the time delay between when data is produced and when it becomes available for consumption — and the DMBOK names six types, which you should be able to order along the spectrum on screen. With the most latency is batch, where data moves in bulk at scheduled intervals, anywhere from hours to days. Next is Change Data Capture, which moves only the changed data, so there's less overhead than a full batch. Then near-real-time, where data is available within seconds to minutes. Then asynchronous, where data moves without waiting for a response. Then synchronous, which is immediate — the calling system waits for a response before proceeding. And with the lowest latency, streaming — a continuous flow. The exam fact to anchor: batch has the highest latency, streaming has the lowest.

1.title: Transformation & ETL vs. ELT
1.text: When you integrate data, you usually transform it to reconcile differences. There are three transformation types. Structural transformation converts formats — say, XML to relational. Semantic transformation reconciles different meanings of the same concept across systems. And calculated or derived transformation applies business rules to compute new values. Now the big distinction, laid out side by side on screen: ETL versus ELT. ETL stands for Extract, Transform, Load — you transform the data before loading it into the target, which is the traditional approach. ELT stands for Extract, Load, Transform — you load the raw data first and then transform it inside the target system. ELT is common in Big Data and data lake environments, but it requires the target system to have substantial processing capacity. So remember: ETL transforms first, ELT loads first.

1.title: Change Data Capture (CDC)
1.text: Change Data Capture, CDC, is an efficient technique that detects and moves only the data that has changed, rather than re-processing everything — which dramatically reduces overhead. There are three main CDC methods. Log-based CDC reads the database's transaction log; it works in near real-time and has minimal impact on the source system, which makes it the best option in most cases. Trigger-based CDC uses database triggers to write changes to a shadow or audit table — but because a trigger fires on every write, it adds overhead to every transaction on the source. And timestamp-based CDC simply queries a last-modified column, which is simple but can miss deletes. The exam point: log-based CDC is the least invasive, while trigger-based CDC burdens the source on every write.

1.title: The 3 Interaction Models
1.text: There are three interaction models for connecting systems, drawn side by side on screen. Point-to-point uses direct connections between systems — it's simple when you have just a few systems, but it becomes unmanageable as you scale. In fact, there's a formula you should memorize: for n systems, point-to-point requires n times n-minus-one, divided by two, unique interfaces. Hub-and-spoke uses a central hub that receives and routes all data, which dramatically reduces the number of connections — but the hub becomes a single point of failure. And publish-subscribe has publishers post data to topics, with subscribers receiving only the data they care about, providing loose coupling between systems. One key exam fact about pub-sub: multiple independent subscribers can each receive their own copy of an event — that's what distinguishes it from a simple queue.

1.title: Architecture Patterns
1.text: Let's cover four architecture patterns. The Enterprise Service Bus, or ESB, is a middleware layer that coordinates messaging between services — it handles routing, transformation, and protocol translation, and it's a core component of Service-Oriented Architecture. Service-Oriented Architecture, SOA, is an architecture where services are loosely coupled, interoperable, and reusable, exposed through standard interfaces like web services, which lets you share business functions across systems. Complex Event Processing, CEP, processes many events in real time to identify patterns and trigger responses — a classic use case is fraud detection. And Data-as-a-Service, DaaS, delivers data via a web service on demand, isolating data management from the consumers. The relationship to remember: the ESB is the messaging backbone of SOA, and CEP is your real-time event pattern engine.

1.title: Exchange Standards & the Canonical Model
1.text: When systems exchange data, standards reduce chaos. The canonical model is the big idea here — it's a common, enterprise-wide data model used as the standard for data exchange. Instead of building N-times-N-minus-one point-to-point mappings between every pair of systems, each system simply maps to and from the single canonical model, which collapses an enormous amount of complexity. NIEM, the National Information Exchange Model, is the US Federal framework and methodology for developing data exchanges between organizations — and an important exam nuance is that NIEM is a standard and methodology, not a technology. And for formats, XML is widely used for structured and semi-structured data, while JSON is lightweight and preferred for web services and NoSQL. The headline concept: a canonical model replaces many point-to-point mappings with one shared model.

1.title: Data Hubs & Interaction Points
1.text: Let's distinguish three shared-storage hubs, because the exam likes to contrast them. An Operational Data Store, or ODS, is an integration point for operational systems holding current, near-real-time data. A Data Warehouse holds integrated, historical, subject-oriented data for analysis. And a Data Lake stores raw data in its native format, applying schema only at read time — schema-on-read. On the interaction-point side, you have APIs, which define how systems interact; web services, which expose functionality over HTTP using SOAP or REST; and message queues, which hold messages between systems to enable asynchronous communication — and because they use persistent storage, they can guarantee delivery. So: ODS is current and operational, the warehouse is historical and analytical, and the lake is raw and schema-on-read.

1.title: The 5 Activities
1.text: DII has five activities. First, define the DII architecture — assess the current state, define the target, select the appropriate interaction models, and define your exchange standards and canonical models. Second, design the data integration solutions — capture the source-to-target mapping requirements, define the transformation rules, and establish error handling and logging. Third, develop the solutions — implement the ETL or ELT processes, build and test the data services, and document the data lineage. Fourth, implement the data flows — deploy and schedule the processes, monitor them, and handle exceptions. And fifth, maintain and monitor — track latency, throughput, and error rates, and manage changes to source and target schemas. Two deliverables to remember: source-to-target mappings and data lineage.

1.title: Governance & Metrics
1.text: Governance for DII centers on a few concerns: data lineage, tracking data from source to target; transformation-rule management, making sure business rules are documented and approved; error-handling standards, so failed integrations are handled consistently; and metadata management, especially the source-to-target mappings and technical lineage. For metrics, you watch latency — actual versus target delivery time; data quality, measured by error rates in the integration processes; availability of the integration services; volume, the records processed per unit time; and rejects, the number of records that fail validation. The takeaway: DII leans heavily on metadata, particularly mappings and lineage, to stay governable.

1.title: Key Numbers & Quick Facts (Cheat Sheet)
1.text: Let's consolidate. DII has three goals and three guiding principles — re-use, abstraction, and shared responsibility. There are six latency types, with batch the highest and streaming the lowest. There are three interaction models, and point-to-point follows the formula n times n-minus-one over two. ETL transforms then loads; ELT loads then transforms, used in data lakes. The best CDC method is log-based. The ESB is the messaging backbone of SOA. A canonical model replaces N-times-N-minus-one mappings with one shared model. And NIEM is the US Federal exchange standard and methodology. Review these until they're instant.

1.title: Common Exam Traps
1.text: Here are the traps. First, don't equate integration with interoperability — integration consolidates data, while interoperability is about systems communicating. Second, streaming does not have the most latency; batch does, and streaming has the least. Third, ETL and ELT are not the same — ELT loads the raw data first and is used in data lakes, while ETL transforms first. Fourth, trigger-based CDC is not the least invasive; log-based CDC is, because it reads the transaction log instead of firing on every write. And fifth, hub-and-spoke does have a weakness — the hub is a single point of failure. And don't forget to memorize the point-to-point formula, n times n-minus-one over two.

1.title: Module Summary
1.text: Let's wrap up. Data Integration and Interoperability moves and consolidates data within and between systems — integration consolidates, interoperability communicates. There are six latency types, with batch the most and streaming the least, and three interaction models: point-to-point, governed by the n-times-n-minus-one-over-two formula; hub-and-spoke, where the hub is a single point of failure; and publish-subscribe, with loose coupling. ETL transforms first while ELT loads first for data lakes, and log-based CDC is the least invasive change-capture method. The ESB powers SOA, CEP handles real-time patterns, and a canonical model slashes mapping complexity. And the whole discipline is governed through lineage, source-to-target mappings, and metadata. That's Chapter 8.

1.title: Let's Test Your Knowledge
1.text: Time for five practice questions on data integration and interoperability. These focus on the change-data-capture methods, ETL transformations, and the difference between publish-subscribe and a point-to-point queue. Read each carefully, pick your answer, and then reveal the solution. Here we go.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one: you need to capture every insert, update, and delete in near real-time with minimal impact on the source. Which CDC method? The answer is A — log-based CDC, which reads the transaction log to capture all change types with minimal source load. Snapshot diffs are heavy, timestamp queries miss deletes, and triggers add overhead.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two: what's the primary drawback of trigger-based CDC versus log-based? The answer is B — it adds overhead to every write transaction on the source, because the trigger fires on each modification. Log-based CDC avoids that by reading the already-written log.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three: an ETL process corrects misspelled cities, trims spaces, and standardizes phone formats. Which transform type? The answer is C — cleansing and standardization. Partitioning splits data, aggregation summarizes it, and enrichment adds external data — none of which is happening here. Two more on the next slide.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four: in publish/subscribe, how does publishing an event to a topic differ from a point-to-point message queue? The answer is C — in pub/sub, multiple independent subscribers can each receive a copy of the event. A point-to-point queue delivers each message to just a single consumer. That fan-out, with loose coupling, is the defining feature of pub/sub. Question five: a downstream service is temporarily down, and the platform holds messages until it recovers. Which property makes that possible? The answer is B — guaranteed delivery with persistent message storage. Because the queue stores messages durably, it retains them until the consumer is available again. Synchronous semantics, by contrast, would fail or block when the consumer is down. That completes Module 8. Next up is Module 9, Document and Content Management, where we move from structured data into the world of unstructured content and records. I'll see you there.
